summary: Source Description (SDES) items are normally sent in RTCP, but sometimes they need to arrive faster, for example when a new source joins an RTP session and receivers need to know who it is. This proposed standard defines an RTP header extension that carries SDES items in the media packets themselves, speeding up delivery.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7941 lets RTP packets carry selected source-description information that would otherwise arrive in RTCP. This can help receivers identify and synchronize a new media source sooner.

subtitle: Carries selected RTCP source-description items in RTP headers for faster delivery.

tldr.problem: RTCP source-description items such as CNAME may arrive too late for a receiver to identify and synchronize a new RTP source.
tldr.mechanism: An RTP header extension carries selected SDES items as UTF-8 text using the one-byte or two-byte element format defined for RTP header extensions.
tldr.outcome: The extension complements RTCP and is intended only for items needing timely delivery. RFC 7941 was updated by RFC 8843 and RFC 9143.

today: RFC 7941 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2016. It has been updated by RFC 8843 and RFC 9143, and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Send SDES Items with RTP
sections.content:
RTCP normally carries Source Description (SDES) items. When a new synchronization source joins an RTP session, a receiver may need information such as CNAME before it can relate that source to other streams or synchronize playback.

RFC 7941 defines an RTP header extension for selected SDES items. It complements RTCP rather than replacing it. Not every SDES item belongs in the extension: the RFC identifies privacy-sensitive items such as Name and Location and says they generally do not need to arrive with the first RTP packets.
sections.plainLanguage: A receiver may need a source's CNAME before it can synchronize related media. Carrying selected SDES items in RTP can deliver that information sooner than waiting for RTCP.

sections.title: One-Byte and Two-Byte Formats
sections.content:
The extension uses the general RTP header extension mechanism. In the one-byte form, a 4-bit ID is followed by a 4-bit length; the data contains the length value plus one bytes of UTF-8 text, allowing 1 to 16 bytes.

In the two-byte form, an 8-bit ID and an 8-bit length precede UTF-8 data of 0 to 255 bytes. Signaling maps each extension ID to an SDES item type through a registered URN. One SSRC cannot mix the one-byte and two-byte formats, so a value needing the longer format requires other extensions in that stream to use it too.
sections.plainLanguage: The one-byte form carries 1 to 16 bytes of text, while the two-byte form carries 0 to 255 bytes. A stream uses one format consistently rather than mixing the two.

sections.title: Choosing and Repeating Header Extensions
sections.content:
Adding SDES information increases RTP packet size. The RFC advises packetizers to account for extension bytes so packets do not exceed the path MTU and cause IP fragmentation. Senders should include extensions only when needed instead of repeating them in every packet throughout a session.

The number and timing of repetitions depend on packet loss and how soon receivers need the information. For a new SSRC, the sender aims for a high chance that participants receive it. For a late joiner, a sender or middlebox can target the new receiver. RTCP continues to carry SDES items, but a separate RTCP packet does not share delivery fate with the related media packet.
sections.plainLanguage: Header extensions add bytes to media packets, so senders should account for the extra size and repeat information only as often as needed. Sending it with media ties its arrival to that media packet.

sections.title: Handling Updates from RTP and RTCP
sections.content:
An SDES value can arrive through both RTP and RTCP. Packet reordering or separate RTP and RTCP processing paths can cause an older value to arrive after a newer one.

Receivers can use sequence numbers to reject RTP extension values that are not newer than the last applied value. They can also compare the approximate send time in an RTCP sender report with the last RTP packet carrying the item. The RFC cautions that pacing can make timestamps differ from actual transmission time.
sections.plainLanguage: When the same item arrives through RTP and RTCP, an older packet could arrive late. A receiver can compare sequence numbers or approximate send times before replacing its current value.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
SDES items can reveal private information or help profile software. The privacy impact of CNAME depends on how it is generated: a short-lived random value has different implications from a value containing a user and host name or a device address.

If RTCP has confidentiality protection, the corresponding SDES header extensions MUST also be protected. The RFC recommends strong integrity protection and source authentication because changing an item could make an application associate the wrong streams.
sections.plainLanguage: Source descriptions can identify a person, device or software. Protect the extension's confidentiality and integrity when the corresponding RTCP information is protected.

sections.title: SDES Extension Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the base URN urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:sdes and created a subregistry for RTP SDES compact header extensions. The initial registered item is CNAME, under urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:sdes:cname.

Future registrations need a corresponding SDES item registration, security and privacy considerations, and an explanation of why timely delivery requires a header extension instead of RTCP alone.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry lists SDES items allowed in this RTP extension. A new item must explain why it needs faster delivery and describe its privacy and security issues.
